newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia seals Chechen deal, targets rent reform.
newsitem.headline: Russia seals Chechen deal, targets rent reform.

text.p: Russian President Boris Yeltsin, promising to remember the poor in a new era of economic reform, sealed a peace deal with separatist Chechnya on Monday and prepared for a crucial round of consultations with NATO leaders.

Yeltsin said the peace agreement he signed with Chechen leader Aslan Maskhadov would end 400 years of conflict between Russia and the Moslem Caucasus region, which has long resented rule from Moscow and still seeks full independence.
"We have signed a peace deal of historic dimensions, putting a full stop to 400 years of history," Yeltsin said after the signing ceremony, which was broadcast on Russian television.
"Some kind of war was going on throughout this period and the people felt insecure."
Yeltsin, re-elected last July for a second term in office, has admitted that his failed effort to crush Chechnya's independence bid by force was one of his worst political mistakes.
Tens of thousands of people, most of them civilians, were killed in 21 months of fighting before Russia's troops pulled back in humiliation last year.
The army is still smarting from the wounds. Morale is low and soldiers have not been paid for months. The government, short of cash, cannot afford to pay its bills or buy supplies.

Russia's Finance Ministry, in a letter quoted by Interfax news agency, told parliament on Monday that the government spent $292 million to rebuild the Kremlin building housing Yeltsin's office and his administration. Foreign contractors were paid $179 million and Russian contractors $112 million.

Officials say massive tax arrears and tax evasion are the main reasons for the cash crunch and Yeltsin is examining a draft decree that state employees should declare their income and give full information about their property, shares and bank accounts.

The decree, "On some measures to avert corruption and the abuse of power in the civil service", has been prepared by First Deputy Prime Minister Boris Nemtsov, who is leading both the housing reform plans and the government's anti-corruption drive.
The government, determined to cut spending, has targeted the bottomless pit of subsidies for housing and communal services in the next round of the economic reform programme.
Yeltsin, making a rare appearance at a government meeting, said the changes were as important a part of government plans as the 1992-94 drive to hand state-owned firms over to the public.
He told a government meeting that mistakes had been made in the privatisation programme, but added: "We do not have the right to make mistakes (in housing reform); they will be too expensive."
Yeltsin's intervention shows the importance given to the reforms, which will replace across-the-board housing subsidies with targeted grants. "The poor must only gain from these reforms," he said.

But the changes could be as painful for millions of Russians as Yeltsin's decision at the start of market reforms in 1992 to free subsidised Soviet-era prices, a move which unleashed inflation and wiped away the value of people's savings.
Yeltsin put the cost of housing subsidies at a staggering 119 trillion roubles a year -- equivalent to four percent of gross domestic product or 30 percent of public sector spending.
"This money is being spent ineffectively and unfairly," he said in remarks broadcast on Russian Public Television.

Russians, enjoying a privilege inherited from Soviet times, pay very low rents by international standards. A one-bedroomed state-owned apartment in a prestigious Moscow district could cost around 120,000 roubles, or just over $20 a month.
Foreigners, often renting the same apartments from the tenants or from individuals who have privatised the property, could pay up to $2,000.
Yeltsin's next main challenge is the response to NATO's plans to invite membership from countries who were Moscow's Warsaw Pact allies in Cold War days.

The presidential press office said on Monday that Yeltsin would telephone the leaders of several NATO states this week to discuss final details on a new security agreement with the alliance. The deal is due to be signed in Paris on May 27.
NATO Secretary General Javier Solana is due in Moscow on Tuesday for talks with Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov.
The Moscow-NATO deal is aimed at overcoming Russia's strong objections to the alliance's plans to expand eastwards.
Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic are thought to be top of the list to join, but Romania and Slovenia also hope to be in the first wave of new members.
($1 = 5,750 roubles
